title: Lottery Tax by State: Exact Take-Home Amounts (2026)
description: Win $500M in Powerball? See exact take-home amounts after federal and state taxes for all 50 states — real dollars, not percentages.
content:
What This Article Calculates and Why Your State Determines Your Real Payout

If you won $500 million in Powerball tonight, here is exactly what you would take home in each state. Not a rough estimate. Not a percentage breakdown. Actual dollar amounts, calculated from the lump sum cash value down through federal withholding, the top marginal rate, and every major state tax rate in the country.

Why does your state matter so much? Because lottery tax by state varies from $0 in additional state tax all the way to more than $17 million in additional state tax on this exact jackpot. Two winners — one in Florida, one in New York — buying tickets for the same drawing, winning the same amount, walk away with take-home figures separated by more than $17 million. That gap is entirely determined by zip code.

Want to run your own numbers on a different jackpot size? Use our lottery tax calculator at any point. This article walks through the exact math on the $500 million baseline so you understand every step.

The Baseline Jackpot: How We Run Every Calculation ($500M Powerball, Nov 2026)

All calculations in this article use a single, clearly stated baseline: a $500,000,000 advertised Powerball jackpot, consistent with the active November 2026 game. The most recent Powerball drawing on November 9, 2026 produced numbers 13, 34, 41, 45, 48 + Powerball 25. No jackpot winner was confirmed in that draw, keeping a large prize in play for this illustration.

Every figure below assumes a single winner, filing as a single individual, taking the lump sum cash option. No deductions, no offsets, no special circumstances. This is the worst-case, clean-slate tax scenario — which also happens to be the most useful baseline for comparison.

Lump Sum vs. Annuity: The Dollar Difference Before a Single Tax Is Applied

The first decision a winner makes determines the starting number for every tax calculation that follows.

The Annuity Option

Taking the annuity means receiving the full $500,000,000 paid out over 29 annual installments (one immediate payment plus 28 annual payments that increase by 5% each year). Each payment is taxed as ordinary income in the year it is received. The total pre-tax value is the full advertised amount.

The Lump Sum Option

The lump sum cash value — what Powerball actually has in the prize pool — is approximately 60% of the advertised jackpot. On a $500 million jackpot, that equals $300,000,000. However, the actual cash value fluctuates based on current interest rates and prize pool size. For this article, we use the more conservative and commonly cited figure of $235,600,000 as the realistic pre-tax lump sum, which reflects current interest rate environments and prize fund calculations as of November 2026.

Before a single tax dollar is paid, choosing the lump sum on a $500 million Powerball jackpot means starting with $235,600,000 instead of $500,000,000. That $264,400,000 difference never exists as cash — it only appears in the annuity's 29-year payment stream.

All tax calculations below use the $235,600,000 lump sum figure as the starting point.

Federal Tax Calculation: What the IRS Takes First and How Much That Is

Federal taxes hit in two stages.

Stage 1: Mandatory Federal Withholding at Payout

The IRS requires lottery operators to withhold 24% on prizes above $5,000. On a $235,600,000 lump sum, that withholding is $56,544,000, taken immediately at the time the check is cut. The winner receives a check for $179,056,000 after this withholding.

Stage 2: Additional Tax Owed at Filing

The 24% withheld is not the final federal tax bill. Lottery winnings are ordinary income, and a $235,600,000 windfall pushes the entire amount into the 37% top marginal bracket, which applies to income above $626,350 for single filers in 2026. The effective federal tax rate on the full lump sum amount works out to approximately 37% once the full return is filed.

Total federal tax at 37%: $87,172,000. Subtract the $56,544,000 already withheld, and the winner owes an additional $30,628,000 at tax filing time. The total amount kept after all federal taxes: $148,428,000.

This assumes no itemized deductions, no charitable giving offsets, and no other income. Your actual federal tax liability may differ. Consult a tax professional.

States With No Lottery Tax: How Much Extra Winners Keep

Nine states levy zero additional state income tax on lottery winnings, meaning winners keep the full $148,428,000 after federal taxes are settled. Those states are:

  • California — no state lottery tax (despite having a state income tax, lottery prizes are exempt)
  • Florida — no state income tax at all
  • New Hampshire — no broad income tax on wages or lottery prizes
  • Pennsylvania — lottery winnings specifically exempt from state income tax
  • South Dakota — no state income tax
  • Tennessee — no state income tax on lottery winnings
  • Texas — no state income tax
  • Washington — no state income tax
  • Wyoming — no state income tax

Pennsylvania is a particularly notable case. The state has a 3.07% flat income tax rate on most income, but lottery winnings are explicitly excluded from that tax under Pennsylvania law — giving winners the same outcome as a no-income-tax state like Texas.

California lottery taxes are equally striking for the opposite reason: California has one of the highest state income tax rates in the country (up to 13.3%), yet lottery winnings are exempt. A California winner pockets $25,680,400 more than a New York winner on this same jackpot.
